When we describe how an object moves in a way that obeys Newton's second law, we must remember that all objects are actually made of constituent particles, i.e. not a single piece. There are many different types of particles, and they are generally not distributed uniformly in the object. An extended object might change shape as it moves, like a water balloon or a cat falling. This implies that the constituent particles are applying internal forces on each other, in addition to the external force that is acting on the object as a whole. The problem is to determine what part of an extended object is obeying Newton's second law when an external force is applied. We also need to determine how the motion of the object as a whole is affected by both the internal and external forces. A Khan Academy video is linked on the course webpage. The center of mass is the mass-weighted average position of a system. As you watch, notice how heavier objects pull the center of mass closer to themselves. This same idea applies whether the system is two particles, the Earth Moon system, or a complicated object made of many pieces. Internal and external forces. Second, determine the location of each particle in x, y, and z coordinates relative to a reference location, usually the origin. Third, determine the mass of each particle and the total summed mass, including any mass at the origin. Fourth, calculate the r sub-center of mass x, r sub-center of mass y, and r sub-center of mass z coordinates. If required, use the Pythagorean theorem to determine its magnitude. The model, we treat the Earth Moon system as two point masses separated by the average Earth Moon distance, and we ignore gravitational interactions with all other bodies. Center of mass conservation of momentum. Suppose you have n objects with masses m sub 1, m sub 2, and so on through m sub n. And initial velocities vector v sub 1, vector v sub 2, and so on through vector v sub n. The center of mass of the objects is vector r sub center of mass equals 1 over m times the sum from j equals 1 to n of m sub j vector r sub j. And its velocity is vector v sub center of mass equals d vector r sub center of mass divided by dt, which equals 1 over m times the sum from j equals 1 to n of m sub j times d vector r sub j divided by dt. Thus, the initial momentum of the center of mass is the quantity m times d vector r sub center of mass divided by dt initially equals the sum from j equals 1 to n of m sub j times d vector r sub j initially divided by dt. Equivalently, m vector v sub center of mass initial equals the sum from j equals 1 to n of m sub j vector v sub j initial. After these masses move and interact with each other, the momentum of the center of mass is m vector v sub center of mass final equals the sum from j equals 1 to n of m sub j vector v sub j final. But conservation of momentum tells us that m vector v sub center of mass final equals m vector v sub center of mass initial. So, vector v sub center of mass final equals vector v sub center of mass initial. This implies that conservation of momentum is expressed in terms of the center of mass of the system. Since m represents the mass of the entire system of particles, it is necessarily constant. In the absence of an external force, the velocity of the center of mass never changes. Note, the individual momentum of a single particle is free to move around, accelerate in various directions and with various magnitudes in accordance with the net internal force acting on that object at any time. Such a particle's momentum will not be constant, but the momentum of the entire extended object will be.
